reason: The cited evidence (E1) directly supports reduced friction and wear with WC addition at room temperature, and (E2) supports laser cladding as a viable method for WC-HEA composites, but neither passage provides any evidence for the formation of a lubricious tribofilm or for performance across a wide temperature range up to 800 °C. The key mechanistic and high-temperature premises are therefore unsupported by the cited passages.
premises: Adding WC particles to an HEA matrix reduces friction coefficient under dry sliding
Adding WC particles to an HEA matrix drastically reduces wear volume (e.g., 30 wt.% WC reduces wear to ~3% of pure matrix)
Laser cladding can produce metallurgically bonded WC-HEA composite coatings with high hardness and wear resistance
The friction and wear reduction from WC addition is mediated by a lubricious tribofilm and microstructural reinforcement
These benefits persist across a wide temperature range up to ~800 °C
